metadata.teaching_provenance: RCET3373-planning F26 W03D04 PIC16F883 Interrupts and Context Saving

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an interrupt **flag** from an interrupt **enable** on the PIC16F883?

choices.text: The flag records that the event/request occurred; the enable controls whether that request can reach interrupt service.
choices.rationale: The event flag and the interrupt enable have different jobs.

choices.text: The enable records that the event occurred; the flag selects the interrupt priority.
The flag and enable are two names for the same bit.
The flag saves W while the enable saves STATUS.

feedback.correct: Correct. Think event/request versus permission to interrupt.
feedback.incorrect: Separate the hardware event from the permission gate: the flag records the request and the enable controls whether it can cause service.

questions.solution: The durable model is event -> flag -> enable gates -> CPU interrupt entry. A flag can record an event even when the corresponding interrupt is masked.
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

questions.stem: An interrupt source flag can become set while its individual interrupt enable or `GIE` is clear.

feedback.correct: Correct. Masking the interrupt request does not necessarily prevent the hardware event flag from being set.
feedback.incorrect: The event flag and the enable gate are separate. A pending flag can exist while service is masked.

questions.solution: The flag records the event/request independently of whether the request is currently allowed through the interrupt-enable gates. This is why stale flags matter before enabling interrupts.
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

questions.stem: Match each external-interrupt control with its role for `RB0/INT`.

pairs.target: Selects which RB0/INT edge triggers the request

questions.solution: `INTF` records the event, `INTE` enables the source, and `INTEDG` selects the triggering edge.
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

questions.stem: Which state is automatically saved by PIC16F883 hardware when an interrupt is accepted?

choices.text: The return program counter on the hardware stack
choices.rationale: Interrupt entry preserves the return address so execution can resume.

choices.text: W and STATUS in common RAM
Every SFR used by main
The active interrupt source flag

feedback.correct: Correct. The return PC is automatically stacked; other processor context may require software preservation.
feedback.incorrect: Do not confuse the hardware return stack with software context storage. The device automatically stacks the return PC.

questions.solution: Interrupt entry pushes the return PC onto the hardware stack and vectors execution to `0x0004`. W and STATUS are not automatically preserved for the program by this mechanism.
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

questions.stem: What does `RETFIE` do that an ordinary `RETURN` does not?

choices.text: It returns from the interrupt and re-enables global interrupts by setting `GIE`.
It automatically clears every interrupt source flag.
It saves W and STATUS before returning.
It resets the hardware stack.

feedback.correct: Correct. The source condition must already be serviced correctly before `RETFIE` re-enables interrupt acceptance.
feedback.incorrect: `RETFIE` is an interrupt return, not a generic flag-clearing or context-saving instruction.

questions.solution: `RETFIE` returns using the stacked PC and sets `GIE`. If the source request is still pending, re-enabling interrupts can lead directly back into service.
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

questions.stem: Place these ISR responsibilities in a safe conceptual order for the PIC16F883 single-vector model.
items: Identify the requesting source from its flag(s)
Service the source and leave its request condition resolved
questions.solution: A robust single-vector pattern is save context -> identify source -> service/clear -> restore context -> `RETFIE`. Multiple source handlers can funnel to one common restore/exit path.
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

questions.stem: Why is common RAM such as `0x70-0x7F` useful for temporary interrupt context storage on the PIC16F883?

choices.text: The same common RAM addresses are accessible without first depending on a particular bank selection.
Common RAM is part of the hardware return stack.
Values in common RAM are automatically restored by `RETFIE`.
Only interrupt code can access common RAM.

feedback.correct: Correct. Context save code should avoid creating a bank-selection dependency before the original STATUS has been preserved.
feedback.incorrect: Common RAM is ordinary data memory, not the return stack and not automatically restored. Its useful property here is bank-independent accessibility.

questions.solution: Using common RAM for `W_TEMP`/`STATUS_TEMP` avoids needing to change bank state merely to reach the temporary storage locations while the original STATUS is being preserved.
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

questions.stem: Why does the Microchip context-save pattern use `SWAPF` while preserving/restoring STATUS instead of relying on `MOVF STATUS,W`?

choices.text: `SWAPF` can move the value without changing STATUS flags, while `MOVF` can affect Z before STATUS is safely preserved.
`SWAPF` automatically pushes STATUS onto the hardware stack.
`MOVF` cannot read STATUS.
`SWAPF` disables interrupts until `RETFIE`.

feedback.correct: Correct. The save/restore sequence must avoid changing the very status bits it is trying to preserve.
feedback.incorrect: Inspect the instruction effects: `MOVF` can affect Z, while `SWAPF` is useful in this sequence because it does not alter STATUS flags.

questions.solution: The temporary swapped form is a means of transferring/restoring the value without modifying STATUS flags during the save/restore sequence. The later swap restores the original nibble order.
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

source.section: 14.4 Context Saving During Interrupts; Example 14-1; instruction descriptions

questions.stem: An ISR services `RB0/INT` but returns with `INTF = 1`. `INTE` is still set. What is the most likely behavior once `RETFIE` sets `GIE` again?

choices.text: The interrupt request can immediately send execution back through interrupt entry because the source is still pending.
The processor ignores `INTF` until Reset because the ISR has already run once.
`RETFIE` automatically clears `INTF`, so nothing unusual occurs.
The return PC is lost because the flag is still set.

feedback.correct: Correct. A pending enabled request can be serviced again as soon as global interrupt acceptance is restored.
feedback.incorrect: Trace the request path after `RETFIE`: source flag still set + source enable set + GIE restored means the request is still eligible.

questions.solution: The source condition must be resolved before the common exit. With `INTF`, `INTE`, and restored `GIE` all active, the CPU can immediately re-enter interrupt service.
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

questions.stem: At `FOSC = 4 MHz`, the external-interrupt latency is 3 to 4 instruction cycles. What is the **maximum** nominal latency in microseconds?

feedback.correct: Correct. At 4 MHz, one instruction cycle is 1 us, so four cycles is 4 us.
feedback.incorrect: First calculate `FCY = FOSC/4`; at 4 MHz that gives a 1 us instruction cycle. Then use the upper end of the 3-4 cycle latency range.

questions.solution: `FCY = 4 MHz / 4 = 1 MHz`, so `TCY = 1 us`. The maximum of the stated 3-4 cycle latency is `4 * 1 us = 4 us`.
questions.author: Tim Rossiter
